fuzzy_decision_model.summary: A first-order Takagi-Sugeno system: Gaussian terms on the most informative features, Wang-Mendel rules with linear consequents, tuned by ANFIS hybrid learning.
fuzzy_decision_model.implementationNote: Bridge: the TSK output (+1 up / -1 down target) becomes P(up) through a validation curve; the price model is the same system fitted to the scaled move. Differs from the spec: rules are learned from training bars, inputs capped so rules stay populated. Expect: a smooth, locally linear score.

input_feature_count.label: Inputs
input_feature_count.description: Feature columns used as fuzzy inputs (most training mutual information).

rule_count.label: Rules kept
rule_count.description: Wang-Mendel antecedents kept, by training coverage.

epochs.label: Epochs
epochs.description: Hybrid-learning passes (least squares, then a gradient step).

learning_rate.label: Learning rate
learning_rate.description: Gradient step on the membership centres and widths.

regularization_strength.label: Ridge penalty
regularization_strength.description: Ridge penalty of the consequent least-squares solve, per training bar.

patience.label: Patience
patience.description: Epochs without validation improvement before stopping.

native.produces: Each indicator value is given a degree of membership in overlapping linguistic terms (low, medium, high), every if-then rule fires with a strength taken from those degrees, and the fired rules are blended and defuzzified into one crisp decision value per bar together with the per-rule firing strengths.
native.targetVariable: a graded decision for the bar, such as a position-size multiplier or a confidence score, expressed as one crisp number that changes smoothly as the indicators cross their term boundaries
native.objectiveNote: A hand-designed rule base minimises nothing because an expert sets the membership boundaries; only the adaptive neuro-fuzzy variant tunes those boundaries and the rule consequents by gradient descent on a squared error against a labelled target.

metrics.why: A fuzzy rule base only decides where its membership functions overlap the bar's indicator values, so the share of bars on which some rule fires above the firing threshold, and the share each rule owns, shows whether the linguistic terms actually cover the market or leave it to a default.

Each rule is a readable claim such as strong trend with low volatility means a large position, and the claim is tested by whether the bars where that rule fires most strongly are followed by a different up share than the series as a whole.
metrics.baseline: the up share of all scored bars of the same series

metrics.why: The specification names its own reference: the same rules with crisp thresholds in place of the overlapping membership functions, so the gain is the score of the fuzzy system minus the score of that hard-threshold version built from the same indicators.
metrics.baseline: the same rule base with every membership function replaced by a crisp threshold

metrics.why: The stated risk is rule-base drift, where boundaries tuned in one volatility regime misfire in the next, so the share of refits in which the same rules and nearly the same term boundaries reappear says whether the linguistic knowledge is durable.

The number of term combinations considered as rules grows quickly with the linguistic terms per input, and the more candidate rules were tried against the training bars before the rule base was fixed, the more of its apparent edge is selection luck.

It applies to the adaptive neuro-fuzzy variant only, where an overgrown rule base with heavily overlapping terms fits training noise and the squared error on the validation block pulls away from the squared error on the training bars.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: Natively the system ends at a defuzzified decision value; the Sharpe ratio is an as-run number for the engine's rule applied to the curve-mapped fuzzy output.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: The rule base has no benchmark-relative return and the registry holds no alpha metric; as run the reference is buy and hold on the same folds.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a property of the as-run trading account and not of fuzzification, rule firing and defuzzification.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The fuzzy system holds no portfolio natively; turnover is measured only as run from the engine's closed trades.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It needs a traded return and a drawdown, neither of which a rule base of membership functions produces on its own.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: No loss tail exists for a per-bar crisp decision value and the registry holds no conditional value at risk metric.

notApplicable.name: Held-out log-likelihood
notApplicable.why: Membership degrees are degrees of truth and not probabilities, so the fuzzy system assigns no density to a bar and has no likelihood to score.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is the specification's adaptive neuro-fuzzy Takagi-Sugeno variant only: Gaussian terms on the few feature columns with the most training mutual information, rule antecedents generated from the training bars instead of written by an expert, linear consequents solved by ridge least squares toward a plus-one or minus-one direction target, and a logistic curve fitted on validation rows turning the output into a probability, so the as-run numbers grade a learned smooth score and not an authored linguistic rule base.
asRun.probabilityNote: The normalised product of Gaussian memberships weights each rule's linear consequent, their sum is a score trained toward plus one for up and minus one for down, and a two-parameter logistic curve refitted on the fold's validation rows at every epoch maps that score to the probability of up.

stepQuantity.unit: on training rows the mean squared difference between the fuzzy output and the plus-one or minus-one direction target, and on validation rows nats per scored bar of the curve-mapped output

meaningful.why: The firing-weighted sum of linear consequents is a smooth continuous score, and the fitted curve keeps its order unless the slope is negative, so this ranking number tests the fuzzy system's own ordering of bars free of the curve's scale.

The price forecast is the same Takagi-Sugeno system fitted a second time to the scaled move, used directly with no curve, so its skill against the no-change forecast is the cleanest test of what the membership functions and rule consequents learned.

It grades the stated odds of the fuzzy output after the validation-fitted logistic curve, and the kept epoch was chosen on the validation version of this number, so it measures system plus curve plus that choice on test bars.
A bounded proper score of the same curve-mapped output that does not explode if a bar with unusual inputs drives the linear consequents to an extreme score.
The curve is an unweighted fit on validation rows, so a calibration gap on test bars shows the mapping from fuzzy score to up frequency failing to carry over to the next span.
A least-squares fit toward a plus-one or minus-one target on noisy bars shrinks the output toward zero, and this spread shows how far the mapped probability ever moves from its centre.
The hard call is whether the curve-mapped fuzzy score is at least one half, so it depends on the fitted curve's intercept, which sets the prior, as well as on the rules.
Averaging the hit rate on up bars and down bars stops a curve intercept that leans one way from reading as skill of the fuzzy rules.
One symmetric number for the up or down call of the fuzzy system that stays near zero when the curve calls every bar the same direction.
The second fuzzy system's predicted move in points against the realised horizon move, to be read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same resolved bars.
The sign of the second system's forecast after tick rounding is a direction view with no validation curve, so its gap to accuracy shows what the curve and the separate direction fit changed.
What the engine's rule earned after costs going long when the curve-mapped fuzzy score was at least one half and short otherwise; the graded position size the specification describes is not used.
The fuzzy system's calls against holding the instrument over the same folds, the only same-series trading reference the engine computes.
Per-bar net result of trading the fuzzy call over its variability; zero is an arithmetic marker because a random-direction trader still pays costs.
The deepest fall of the account when every bar's fuzzy call is traded at full size, which is where rule-base drift into an unfamiliar regime would show.
Winning over losing trade totals for the engine's rule; a trade ends when the fuzzy call flips, and a smooth score should flip less often than a crisp threshold.
Share of closed trades that made money after costs, each trade covering a run of bars on which the mapped fuzzy score stayed on one side of one half.
How often the fuzzy call changed side, the direct measure of the whipsaw that overlapping membership functions are meant to reduce.
Shows whether the validation curve's intercept has the fuzzy system calling almost every bar the same direction.
The search over input count, terms per input, rule count and learning rate is scored on inner training blocks by the shared selection objective, an optimistic selection score and not a result.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training channel holds a squared error toward the plus-one or minus-one target and the validation channel holds the logarithmic loss of the curve-mapped score, two different quantities.
With long only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short once it has traded, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the fuzzy system's graded output.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, so it is not a level the fuzzy system could have been compared with in advance.

caveats: The kept epoch is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, and the logistic curve is refitted on those same validation rows at every epoch, so the validation loss is optimistic twice over and is never a result.

The rules are not authored and do not come from the rule library file: their antecedents are the term combinations that best match the most training bars, and the inputs are capped so each rule keeps enough bars.
The price forecast is a second fit of the same system to the scaled move clipped at its training first and ninety-ninth percentiles, with its own epoch chosen on the validation Huber loss.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because horizon targets overlap, so any interval on these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.

Dials in force by default: long only off, holding bars equal to the label horizon, no stop loss, no take profit, one contract; a same-direction call at holding expiry is kept at no cost and the fold's last bar exits at its close.
For roots other than MNQ the cost per side is the MNQ account figure applied as a stated assumption.

multi_criteria_decision_analysis.summary: TOPSIS: the current bar ranked against its trailing window on the most informative signals, weighted by the analytic hierarchy process or entropy.
multi_criteria_decision_analysis.implementationNote: Bridge: the bar's TOPSIS closeness to the ideal (0..1) minus 0.5, calibrated on validation; the price model scales it by a training slope. Differs from the spec: the spec ranks alternatives; here each bar is ranked against training-span ideals (or its trailing window) and P(up) is the calibrated up-rate of that rank. Expect: a weighted composite signal.

criterion_count.label: Criteria
criterion_count.description: Feature columns with the largest training information coefficient.

ideal_reference.label: Ideal reference
ideal_reference.description: Rank the bar against the training span's 5th-95th percentile ideals, or against its own trailing window (fixed: it sets the history requirement).

sequence_length.label: Trailing alternatives
sequence_length.description: Bars in the trailing decision matrix when the ideal reference is the trailing window, the current one included (fixed: it sets the history requirement).

weighting_method.label: Weighting
weighting_method.description: Criterion weights from AHP pairwise ratios of information coefficients, or the entropy method.

native.produces: A ranked list of a finite set of alternatives, each with a closeness coefficient computed from its weighted distance to the ideal and to the worst case across several criteria, plus a consistency ratio when the weights came from pairwise comparisons.
native.targetVariable: The preference order of the listed alternatives, such as candidate instruments or strategies, under criterion weights that a person stated or derived from pairwise judgments
native.objectiveNote: Nothing is fitted to labelled outcomes: the TOPSIS procedure normalises each criterion, applies the stated weights and orders the alternatives by relative closeness to the ideal, so the answer is only as defensible as the weights.

metrics.why: The criterion weights are a judgment call, so the ranking is trusted only if the top alternatives keep their places when each weight is nudged by a plausible margin; a ranking that flips on a small nudge to one weight decided nothing.
metrics.baseline: The ranking produced by the unperturbed weights

metrics.why: When the weights come from pairwise comparisons in the analytic hierarchy process, this ratio shows whether those judgments contradict one another before any alternative is ranked with them.
metrics.baseline: Zero, the value of a perfectly consistent comparison matrix

metrics.why: If the same alternatives come out on top each time the decision matrix is rebuilt on a new period, the ranking reflects the alternatives; if the top set reshuffles every time, it reflects noise in the criterion values.
metrics.baseline: The top set chosen on the first period

metrics.why: Treating each plausible weight set as a scenario, the shortfall of the top-ranked alternative from whichever alternative wins under that weight set shows how costly it is to have picked the wrong weights.
metrics.baseline: Zero shortfall, which is what the top alternative shows under the weights that ranked it first

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The ranking takes no position; a Sharpe ratio can only enter as one of the criterion columns being weighed.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: An ordered list of alternatives has no return and no benchmark, and the registry carries no alpha metric.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: The method outputs closeness scores, not an equity curve, so it has no drawdown of its own.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: No trades are placed by ranking a decision matrix, so turnover never applied.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: Return over drawdown describes a traded account, which a weighted ranking is not.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The weighted distance to the ideal produces no loss distribution, so there is no tail to average.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: A closeness coefficient orders alternatives and is not a probability of anything, so there is nothing for a probability score to grade.

asRun.standInNote: The specification ranks a list of alternatives under weights a person states. The runnable adapter instead treats each bar as the single alternative, picks its criteria as the criterion_count feature columns most correlated with the outcome on training bars, derives the weights either from those same correlations (the analytic hierarchy option) or from the spread of the criteria on the training bars (the entropy option), and scores the bar's TOPSIS closeness to a training-span ideal. The as-run numbers measure that closeness as a direction signal after a validation-fitted logistic curve, not the quality of a ranking.
asRun.probabilityNote: The bar's weighted relative closeness to the ideal, a number between zero and one, has one half subtracted, and a two-parameter logistic curve fitted on the fold's validation bars turns that signed score into the probability of up.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per scored validation bar, one value for the single fit, of the curve-mapped closeness with the curve fitted on those same validation bars; the ranking minimises nothing, so no training value is logged

meaningful.why: The closeness coefficient promises only an ordering, so the direct test is whether bars sitting nearer the ideal on the chosen criteria went up more often than bars sitting nearer the worst case.
It grades the closeness score after the validation curve has turned it into a probability, on a bounded scale that stays readable when the curve keeps every bar near one half.

It scores the same curve-adjusted closeness; the probability scale belongs entirely to the two curve parameters fitted on validation bars, so this is a score of the weighted composite plus that curve.
It asks whether the bars with the very highest closeness to the ideal were really up bars, which is the end of the ranking a top-choice method cares about.

The search over how many criteria the ranking uses and whether their weights come from the analytic hierarchy or the entropy method is scored on inner blocks of the training span by the shared tuning objective, an optimistic selection score and not a result.
The best setting's search score minus the same quantity on the fold's test walk shows how much of the chosen criterion count and weighting looked good by selection and not by the composite's skill.
The stated odds are the validation curve's doing, so a gap on test bars says the mapping from closeness to up share learned on validation bars did not hold.
A weighted composite of weak criteria gives the curve little to work with, and this spread shows whether the probability ever leaves the neighbourhood of one half.

It counts the hard calls made by cutting the curve-adjusted closeness at one half; the cut point on the closeness scale is set by the curve's intercept, not by the midpoint between ideal and worst case.
Averaging the hit rate over rising and falling bars shows whether closeness to the ideal separates them or the curve's intercept sent every call the same way.
One symmetric figure for the calls made from the composite score, which stays near zero when the criteria chosen on training bars stop lining up with direction.
It is what trading the composite's call earned after costs under the engine's rule, long when the curve-adjusted closeness is at least one half and short otherwise.
It relates the per-bar profit from following the weighted composite to its variability; zero is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level because random calls pay costs too.
It shows the worst losing stretch of the composite's call, which arrives when the training-span correlations that chose and oriented the criteria reverse.
It sets the money won against the money lost on the trades opened when the closeness-based call changed side, after costs, and needs the trade count beside it.
It is the share of the composite's closed trades that made money; a trade runs until the call flips or the fold ends, so it is not a per-bar hit rate.

The forecast is the closeness score minus one half multiplied by a single slope fitted through the origin on training bars, so this tests whether distance from the ideal scales with the size of the move at all.
It gives the typical miss in points of that one-slope readout of closeness; with a small slope the forecast hugs zero and this number approaches the no-change error.
It checks the sign of the slope times the closeness score, which uses the midpoint between ideal and worst case as its cut and no validation curve.

The forecast instance picks its criteria by correlation with the size of the move and the direction instance by correlation with the up label, and the direction call also passes through the curve, so this share shows how often the two readings agree.

With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always in a position once it has traded, so this share describes the engine's rule and not the ranking.

caveats: With the analytic hierarchy weighting the pairwise matrix is built from ratios of the criteria's own training correlations, so it is perfectly consistent by construction and the logged consistency ratio is always zero; it checks nothing in this adapter.

The criteria and their orientation are always chosen from correlations with the outcome on the training span, and the weights come from those same correlations under the analytic hierarchy option or from the spread of the criteria on the training bars under the entropy option, which makes the composite a fitted signal and not a ranking under weights stated in advance.
The logistic curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the fold's validation bars and the slope may come out negative, in which case bars closer to the ideal are called down.
With ideal_reference set to trailing_window the bar is ranked against its own last sequence_length bars instead of the training-span percentiles, which changes what closeness means.
The price forecast comes from a second instance that re-selects its criteria against the scaled move, so the forecast line and the direction call can rest on different feature columns.

Horizons of consecutive bars overlap, so intervals on these scores need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance; for roots other than MNQ the costs are the MNQ account figures, and the last bar of each fold exits at its close.

robust_decision_making.summary: A pool of candidate strategies stress-tested across training-span scenarios (blocks, volatility terciles, trend regimes, doubled costs); the robust ones are blended.
robust_decision_making.implementationNote: Bridge: the robustness-weighted blend of the surviving strategies' scores, calibrated on validation. Differs from the spec: scenarios are re-cuts of the training history with cost stress, so deep uncertainty is only as deep as that history. Expect: a conservative ensemble near the base rate.

candidate_strategy_count.label: Candidate strategies
candidate_strategy_count.description: Strategies in the pool (single features, a logistic regression and three rule strategies).

scenario_block_count.label: Scenario blocks
scenario_block_count.description: Contiguous blocks the training span is cut into.

acceptable_utility_threshold.label: Acceptable utility
acceptable_utility_threshold.description: Mean net utility (scaled move units per bar) a scenario outcome must reach to satisfice.

robustness_metric.label: Robustness metric
robustness_metric.description: Share of scenarios satisficed, or the worst regret against each scenario's best strategy.

scenario_discovery_depth.label: Scenario discovery depth
scenario_discovery_depth.description: Depth of the tree that describes where the robust set fails.

native.produces: A robustness score for each candidate strategy, being the share of a large ensemble of structurally different futures in which it performs acceptably, together with a short description of the conditions under which each strategy fails.
native.targetVariable: How each candidate strategy performs across a swept range of deeply uncertain inputs, and which combinations of those inputs make it fall below the acceptable performance threshold
native.objectiveNote: No loss is fitted: every candidate strategy is run through a simulation model under every sampled future, and the strategies are ordered by the share of futures they satisfice or by their worst regret rather than by average performance.

metrics.why: This is the framework's own ranking criterion: out of all the sampled futures, the share in which a candidate strategy stays above the acceptable performance threshold, which rewards holding up everywhere over shining in one assumed future.
metrics.baseline: The same share for the other candidate strategies run through the identical ensemble of futures

metrics.why: For each sampled future it measures how far the chosen strategy fell short of whichever candidate was best there; a robust choice keeps that shortfall small even in the futures that hurt it most.
metrics.baseline: Zero shortfall, which a strategy shows in a future where it is itself the best candidate

metrics.why: The scenario-discovery step draws a small box of conditions said to break the strategy; coverage says what share of all the failing futures actually fall inside that box, so a low value means most failures are still unexplained.
metrics.baseline: The share of failing futures in the whole ensemble that a box covering every future would capture, which is all of them

metrics.why: Density says what share of the futures inside the discovered box really are failures; a box with low density points a hedge at conditions under which the strategy mostly survives.
metrics.baseline: The share of failing futures in the whole ensemble

metrics.why: If redrawing the ensemble of futures with a new seed moves the vulnerability box to different conditions, the box was describing that one sample and should not steer a hedge.
metrics.baseline: The vulnerability conditions found on the first ensemble

metrics.why: The robust strategy's performance averaged over the swept futures is a promise made by the simulation model; subtracting what the strategy then earned on later bars shows whether the uncertainty ranges covered the future that arrived.
metrics.baseline: A gap of zero, where the later bars behaved like the ensemble

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: A simulated Sharpe ratio per strategy and future is an input the acceptability threshold is applied to, not a realised score of the framework.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: The framework ranks candidates by robustness and trades nothing against a benchmark; the registry also has no alpha metric.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: Drawdown appears as a simulated outcome inside each future; the framework itself has no equity curve.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: No orders are generated by sweeping an ensemble of futures, so turnover never applied.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It summarises a single realised path, while the native result is a share of many simulated futures survived.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: A tail average needs one agreed probability distribution over futures, and the framework exists for the case where no such distribution is trusted.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: The specification states that the framework does not predict a single future outcome, so it issues no probability to score.

notApplicable.name: Rank stability under weight perturbation
notApplicable.why: There are no criterion weights to perturb; robustness here is tested by sweeping the uncertain inputs, which the satisficing share and regret already measure.

asRun.standInNote: The adapter keeps the framework's steps, a pool of candidate strategies, an ensemble of scenarios, a satisficing or minimax-regret ranking and a shallow scenario-discovery tree, but its scenarios are re-cuts of the training history (contiguous blocks, volatility terciles and trend regimes, each at the actual and at twice the round-trip cost) and not a sweep of uncertain inputs through a simulation model. The as-run numbers measure the robustness-weighted blend of the surviving strategies' scores as a direction signal after a validation-fitted logistic curve.
asRun.probabilityNote: Each surviving strategy's score is divided by its training standard deviation, the scores are averaged with weights equal to each strategy's robustness across the scenario ensemble, and a two-parameter logistic curve fitted on the fold's validation bars turns that blend into the probability of up.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per scored validation bar, one value for the single fit, of the curve-mapped robust blend with the curve fitted on those same validation bars; selecting strategies by robustness minimises no loss, so no training value is logged

meaningful.why: The strategies were ranked by their robustness across the training scenarios, each scored by its position times the move net of cost, and only the most robust few were kept; this is the same kind of quantity earned by the blended call on test bars the scenarios never contained.
It tests whether the robustness-weighted blend of the surviving strategies' scores ranks rising bars above falling ones, independent of the scale the validation curve gives it.
The whole point of choosing by robustness instead of average performance is to avoid deep holes, so the worst peak-to-trough loss of the blended call on test bars is a direct check of that promise.
It relates the per-bar profit of the robust blend to its variability; zero is an arithmetic marker, not a no-skill level, because a random-direction trader still pays costs.
Every scenario was evaluated at the actual cost and at twice it, so the cost level at which the blended call's test profit would vanish shows whether that cost stress carried over.

The search over the candidate strategy count, the scenario block count, the acceptable utility, the choice between satisficing and minimax regret and the number of robust strategies kept is scored on inner blocks of the training span by the shared tuning objective, an optimistic selection score and not a result.
The best setting's search score minus the same quantity on the fold's test walk shows how much of the chosen robustness rule looked good by selection and not by surviving the later bars.
It scores the blend after the validation curve has given it a probability scale; that scale comes from the curve's two parameters, so this is a score of the blended strategies plus the curve.
A bounded reading of the same curve-adjusted blend, which stays informative when a conservative ensemble keeps the probability close to the base rate.
The odds are the validation curve's doing, so a gap between stated and observed up share on test bars means the mapping from blended score to up share did not carry forward.
Averaging several standardised strategy scores cancels much of their disagreement, and this spread shows whether the blend ever commits away from one half.
It counts the hard calls made by cutting the curve-adjusted blend at one half; note the strategies were selected on net utility of the move and not on this hit rate.
Averaging the hit rate on rising and on falling bars shows whether the surviving strategies separate the two or the curve's intercept leaned every call one way.
One symmetric figure for the blended call's hits and misses, near zero when the strategies that survived the training scenarios stop agreeing with direction.
It compares money won with money lost on the trades opened when the blended score changed sign, after costs, and should be read with the trade count.

It is the share of the blend's closed trades that made money; trades end when the call flips or the fold ends, so it is a per-trade share and not the per-scenario robustness score that ranked the strategies.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Not computed: this model has no price model, so no forecast line is drawn and no skill exists to report.
Not computed: this model has no price model, so there is no forecast whose error could be measured.
Not computed: this model has no price model, so there is no forecast sign to compare with the move.
Selecting strategies by robustness minimises no loss and logs no training value, so there is nothing to subtract from the validation logarithmic loss.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine never goes flat once in a trade, so this share reflects the engine's rule and not the robust blend.

caveats: The scenario ensemble is cut from the fold's own training bars, and the blocks, volatility terciles and trend regimes overlap one another, so the scenarios are not independent futures and the uncertainty explored is only as deep as that history.

The candidate pool includes a logistic regression fitted on every feature of the training bars, which is then judged on scenarios drawn from those same bars, so its robustness is measured in-sample and it can dominate the blend.

Robustness is scored on mean position times scaled move net of cost, while the engine trades the sign of a validation-curve probability with its own holding and exit rule, so the selection utility and the scored profit are related but not identical.
The scenario-discovery tree that describes where the robust set fails is written to the log only; it does not change any call and its coverage and density are not recorded.
The logistic curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the fold's validation bars, so the validation loss is partly in-sample, and the slope is free to come out negative.

Horizons of consecutive bars overlap, so intervals on these scores need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance; for roots other than MNQ the costs are the MNQ account figures, and the last bar of each fold exits at its close.
